opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of my favourite results from the whole project, because it was something we didn't design for at all. It just fell out of the model.

The setup is that the Continuous Thought Machine has these internal "ticks," a kind of internal time dimension that's decoupled from the input. On the maze task we give it an image of the maze and ask it to output the route as a sequence of moves. When you watch the attention over those ticks with plenty of time, it does what you'd hope: it traces the path from the start, step by step, almost like a person running their finger along the corridors.

Then we cut the number of ticks it gets, so it doesn't have enough internal time to trace the whole path one step at a time. It doesn't just fail. It finds a different algorithm. It starts jumping ahead. Its attention leaps forward to a point further along the route, then works backwards to fill in the section it skipped, then leaps forward again. We started calling it a "leapfrogging" strategy.

What I find fascinating is a few things. First, nobody told it to do that. There's no loss term saying "be clever about your compute budget." The pressure of limited thinking time alone produced a qualitatively different and quite sensible strategy. Second, it's interpretable. You can actually see it, which is rare. With most models you're squinting at activations. Here you can watch the attention move around the maze and say, "Oh, it's planning ahead and backfilling." Third, I think it hints at something bigger. If you give a model a native notion of time to think, how it uses that time becomes a meaningful thing to study. Thinking time stops being only about more compute. It becomes a resource the model reasons about and adapts to, and that's much closer to how we think about intelligence in biological systems.

I'll admit there was a bit of a "huh, I didn't expect that" moment when we first saw it. Those moments are why I wanted to do this kind of research in the first place, rather than just scaling up the same architecture again.

r001.rationale: The response says that with fewer internal ticks, the model jumps ahead along the route and works backward to fill in skipped sections, describing the target strategy under constrained thinking time.

fable-5.1.text:
So the thing I keep coming back to is that we never told the model to do what it ends up doing. We trained it on mazes, and when you look at the attention, it's actually tracing the path through the maze step by step, almost like you'd see a person run their finger along it. Nobody put that in. It just falls out of giving the model internal ticks and letting it use them.

But the really fascinating bit is what happens when you take time away from it. If you give it, say, a fixed budget of thought steps, and the maze is longer than that budget allows, it doesn't just fail or spit out garbage. It solves as much of the maze as it can in the time it has, and it stops at the point where it ran out of thinking. And then if you feed that partial solution back in and let it keep going, it just picks up from where it left off and carries on. So it's effectively learned something like a procedure that it can resume.

And that's quite different from how we normally think about neural networks. Usually you've got a fixed depth, a fixed amount of compute per input, and the problem either fits in that or it doesn't. Here the compute has become a resource the model is allocating over the problem. Harder mazes, more ticks. Easier mazes, it's confident earlier and effectively stops. We didn't engineer that either, it's just what happens when the architecture has a notion of time at all, and when the synchronisation between neurons, rather than a static snapshot of activations, is what the output is read from.

I think the honest thing to say is that we don't fully understand why it generalises the way it does. We've trained on mazes of one size and it works on substantially bigger ones, which transformers really struggle with. My intuition is that because the dynamics are doing the work, it's learnt something closer to the algorithm for solving a maze than a lookup over maze-like patterns. But I'd be lying if I said we had that pinned down. That's part of why I find it exciting, it's one of those results where the model's behaviour is telling you something about what representation it's found, and we're still catching up to it.

r001.rationale: The response says the model traces the maze step by step and resumes a partial solution when given more thinking time. It does not state that it jumps ahead and traces path segments backward from those positions.

astra-6.text:
What I find fascinating is that the time constraint changes how they approach the maze. With more time to think, they can explore, go down a route, and backtrack. When you give them less time, they seem to become more direct, almost as though they’re taking shortcuts in their search.

And I’m being a little careful with that language, because we’re interpreting the behaviour. But it suggests that those internal steps are doing useful computation. The interesting question is whether the model can learn to use whatever thinking budget it has—to explore when there’s time, and make a good decision quickly when there isn’t.

r001.rationale: The response describes shorter thinking budgets leading to more direct routes or shortcuts, but does not say the machines jump ahead and trace path segments backward from those positions.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find fascinating is that the thinking time becomes part of the problem. It’s not just, “Can you solve this maze?” It’s, “Can you solve it with this much computation?” With a tight budget, you need to make progress quickly; with more time, you can afford to explore alternatives.

And that raises a really interesting question: are you just watching the same computation run for longer, or does the model actually develop a different strategy depending on how much time it has? That distinction is what I’d want to understand—whether extra thought is buying you a better search process, rather than simply more steps.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how time budgets may affect exploration and strategy, but does not state that the machines solve long mazes by tracing path segments backward from positions they jump ahead to.
